ap_macroeconomics-m01.stem: In the AD-AS model, aggregate demand shifts to the left in an economy initially at its natural rate of unemployment. Which of the following correctly describes the effect on the short-run Phillips curve?

options.text: The SRPC shifts upward (to the right), so unemployment and inflation both rise.
options.why: Describes a negative supply shock, not a fall in AD.

options.text: The SRPC shifts downward (to the left), so unemployment and inflation both fall.
options.why: Describes a favorable supply shock.

options.text: The economy moves along an unchanged SRPC to a point with lower unemployment and higher inflation.
options.why: Reverses the direction of the movement; a fall in AD raises unemployment and lowers inflation.

options.text: The LRPC shifts to the right, so the natural rate rises.
options.why: A demand shock does not change the natural rate.

options.text: The economy moves along an unchanged SRPC to a point with higher unemployment and lower inflation.
options.why: A fall in AD lowers real GDP and the price level, raising unemployment: a movement down along the SRPC.

ap_macroeconomics-m01.stem: In the AD-AS model, short-run aggregate supply shifts to the right. Which of the following correctly describes the effect on the short-run Phillips curve?

options.text: The LRPC shifts to the left, so the natural rate falls.
options.why: A short-run cost change does not change the natural rate by itself.

options.text: The SRPC shifts downward (to the left), so inflation and unemployment both fall.
options.why: A positive supply shock lowers inflation and unemployment together, which is a downward shift of the SRPC.

options.text: The economy moves along an unchanged SRPC to a point with higher inflation and lower unemployment.
options.why: Describes an AD increase, not a rightward SRAS shift.

options.text: There is no effect on the Phillips curve, because the AD curve does not shift.
options.why: Supply shocks shift the SRPC even when AD does not shift.

options.text: The SRPC shifts upward (to the right), so inflation and unemployment both rise.
options.why: Describes a negative supply shock.

ap_macroeconomics-m02.stem: Which of the following combinations of policies would most likely increase interest rates while having an indeterminate effect on real GDP?

options.text: Contractionary fiscal policy (a smaller budget deficit) and contractionary monetary policy.
options.why: This combination gives real GDP a decrease and interest rates an indeterminate change, which does not match the goal.

options.text: Neither policy, because policies do not affect interest rates or real GDP in the short run.
options.why: Ignores that fiscal and monetary policy shift aggregate demand and change interest rates.

options.text: Contractionary fiscal policy (a smaller budget deficit) and expansionary monetary policy.
options.why: This combination gives real GDP an indeterminate change and interest rates a decrease, which does not match the goal.

options.text: Expansionary fiscal policy (a larger budget deficit) and expansionary monetary policy.
options.why: This combination gives real GDP an increase and interest rates an indeterminate change, which does not match the goal.

options.text: Expansionary fiscal policy (a larger budget deficit) and contractionary monetary policy.
options.why: Fiscal expansion and monetary contraction both raise interest rates, while their effects on real GDP are in opposite directions.

ap_macroeconomics-m03.stem: Why does a policy that tries to keep unemployment permanently below the natural rate through higher inflation eventually fail?

options.text: People never change their expectations about inflation, however long it persists.
options.why: Expectations adjust over time.

options.text: Higher inflation lowers the inflation rate that people expect in the long run.
options.why: Higher money growth leads to higher inflation.

options.text: The long-run Phillips curve slopes downward, so the trade-off is permanent.
options.why: The long-run Phillips curve is vertical.

options.text: Higher inflation raises the natural rate of unemployment permanently.
options.why: The natural rate does not rise because of expansionary policy by itself.

options.text: As expectations adjust, the short-run Phillips curve shifts upward and unemployment returns to the natural rate.
options.why: The trade-off exists only in the short run.

ap_macroeconomics-m03.stem: Why does the short-run Phillips curve shift upward when expected inflation rises?

options.text: Workers and firms build higher expected inflation into wages and prices, so inflation is higher at every unemployment rate.
options.why: Higher expected inflation raises inflation at each unemployment rate.

options.text: Higher expected inflation lowers actual inflation at each unemployment rate.
options.why: Higher expected inflation raises actual inflation.

options.text: Higher expected inflation makes the long-run Phillips curve downward sloping.
options.why: The long-run curve stays vertical at the natural rate.

options.text: Higher expected inflation lowers the natural rate of unemployment.
options.why: Expected inflation does not change the natural rate.

options.text: Higher expected inflation moves the economy along the same curve.
options.why: A change in expectations shifts the curve rather than moving along it.
